lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So does psychology actually prove what it says about human minds?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: That is the main worry in Estimating the reproducibility of psychological study. The authors wanted to see if new experiments match old ones.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: And they didn't just guess, they actually copied studies right?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Exactly. They took one hundred existing studies from three psychology journals and ran their own versions.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Did they use the same people or different ones to test if it holds up?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: They used original materials where available but with high powered designs to get clearer answers.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So if the results changed a lot, that means science is shaky?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Not shaky necessarily but the numbers are very different. Replication effects were exactly half the magnitude of the originals.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Half? Like if they found something big before now it's tiny?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes, and ninety seven percent of the original studies had significant results but only thirty six percent did in the new ones.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So most of what was thought true turned out to be wrong?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Mostly yes. If you combine both sets of results without bias only sixty eight percent still show significant effects.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Is there any reason why the new teams failed to get these same numbers?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Statistical tests suggest success depended more on how strong the original evidence was than who ran the study.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So weak studies are just harder to repeat no matter how hard they try?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: That seems likely. The paper notes forty seven percent of original effect sizes fell in the ninety five confidence interval.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Which means half the results could have been just luck originally?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes, and thirty nine percent were subjectively rated as having replicated but most did not match well.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So what should scientists do to fix this mess?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Use stronger evidence from the start and be more careful about which studies they choose to repeat.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Okay so we need to trust less and check harder before believing what we read?
